name: Raymond Fitzgerald
presenting_complaint: Increasing abdominal distension, confusion and mild fever over 3 days

medical_history.social: Drinks approximately 12 standard drinks per day for 30 years, ongoing. Lives alone. Ex-smoker. No IV drug use. No recent travel.
medical_history.family: No known family history of liver disease.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 61-year-old man with known alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C) presents with 3 days of worsening abdominal distension, low-grade fever and increasing confusion noticed by his neighbour. He has tense ascites, is drowsy but rousable (GCS 14) with asterixis. Obs: BP 102/64, HR 106, RR 20, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 37.9. He has a history of varices, prior encephalopathy and ongoing heavy alcohol use.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Timeline of decompensation: 3 days of increasing distension, fever and confusion; establish baseline mental state and functional level
Screen for precipitants of decompensation: fevers/infection, melaena or haematemesis (variceal bleed), constipation, recent diuretic/lactulose non-adherence, sedatives, dehydration
Alcohol history quantified in standard drinks (approx 12/day, ongoing) and time of last drink to anticipate withdrawal
Viral hepatitis risk factors: IV drug use, tattoos, transfusions, sexual history (screen for hepatitis B/C)
Prior decompensation history: previous SBP, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, paracentesis; adherence to lactulose, spironolactone, frusemide and propranolol
Key negatives and red-flag screen: no overt GI bleeding reported, no recent nephrotoxics/NSAIDs, bowel habit and last bowel action, allergy history
objective: Diagnostic ascitic tap (paracentesis) EARLY — send fluid for cell count/differential, MC&S (blood-culture bottles at bedside), albumin, protein; SAAG calculation
Assess for hepatic encephalopathy: GCS, asterixis, orientation, and grade the encephalopathy
Full septic screen: blood cultures, urinalysis/MSU, CXR, plus the ascitic fluid
Abdominal exam: tense ascites, shifting dullness, tenderness/guarding suggesting SBP, hepatosplenomegaly, caput medusae
Bloods: FBC, UEC (renal function for hepatorenal syndrome), LFTs, coags/INR, venous gas + lactate, ammonia, CRP, BGL, group and hold
PR examination and inspect for melaena; stigmata of chronic liver disease (jaundice, spider naevi, palmar erythema)
assessment: Decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C) — identify and treat the precipitant
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) suspected given fever, ascites and encephalopathy — confirm on ascitic neutrophil count >250/mm3
Hepatic encephalopathy (precipitated by infection and/or lactulose non-adherence)
Consider and actively exclude variceal/GI haemorrhage as a precipitant; consider hepatorenal syndrome, alcohol withdrawal and hepatocellular carcinoma
plan: Diagnostic ascitic tap FIRST — do NOT delay it; if neutrophils >250/mm3 treat as SBP
SBP treatment: IV third-generation cephalosporin (e.g. ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily or cefotaxime 2 g IV 8-hourly) PLUS IV albumin 20% (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3) to prevent hepatorenal syndrome
Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose titrated to 2-3 soft bowel actions/day (oral/NG, or enema if drowsy), add rifaximin 550 mg BD, treat the precipitant and avoid sedatives
IV access x2, cautious fluid resuscitation, correct electrolytes; monitor renal function daily for hepatorenal syndrome; withhold nephrotoxics and NSAIDs
Variceal bleed contingency: if melaena/haematemesis or drop in Hb — resuscitate, IV terlipressin, IV ceftriaxone, urgent gastroscopy within 24h and continue non-selective beta-blocker plan
Alcohol withdrawal prophylaxis (symptom-triggered diazepam per CIWA), continue thiamine 100 mg IV/oral (parenteral before glucose), nutritional support
Ongoing ascites management: salt restriction, continue spironolactone +/- frusemide, large-volume paracentesis with albumin cover if tense and symptomatic
Refer gastroenterology/hepatology; admit under medical team; monitor obs, GCS, fluid balance; arrange HCC surveillance and alcohol support/discharge planning

critical_errors: Not performing a diagnostic ascitic tap because the patient 'does not look septic' — this misses spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Giving broad-spectrum antibiotics WITHOUT first obtaining the diagnostic paracentesis, losing the diagnosis and cell count
Missing or failing to actively exclude variceal haemorrhage as a precipitant of decompensation
Prescribing sedatives/benzodiazepines routinely or nephrotoxics/NSAIDs that worsen encephalopathy and precipitate hepatorenal syndrome
must_not_miss: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (diagnostic paracentesis performed BEFORE antibiotics; albumin given)
Variceal/GI haemorrhage considered and excluded as the precipitant
Hepatic encephalopathy treated with lactulose and precipitant addressed
Hepatorenal syndrome risk mitigated (albumin cover, avoid nephrotoxics, monitor renal function)
